title: Asking for Help
keyIdea: When you are stuck, have a go first: try another way, then look for a clue. If you are still stuck, ask a friend or a grown-up, and say what you tried and what you need, such as a clue. If you are hurt, unsafe or someone is unkind, get a grown-up straight away. Asking after trying is what good learners do.

kid: Everyone gets stuck. Grown-ups get stuck too.
First, have a go. Try a new way. Look for a clue, like a word on the wall.
Still stuck? Ask a friend or a grown-up. Say what you tried. Ask for a clue, not the answer.
If you are hurt, or someone is unkind, get a grown-up right away. You do not need to try first.
adult: Knowing when and how to ask is a learning skill, not a weakness. Research on help-seeking separates two kinds. One is asking for a hint or an explanation so you can finish the job yourself, which goes with better learning. The other is asking someone to do it for you. Many UK classrooms teach a routine such as brain, book, buddy, boss: think, look for a clue, ask a friend, then ask the teacher.

For five- and six-year-olds the aim is a simple order: have a go, try a different way, look for a clue, then ask. Children this age also need a clear exception. If they are hurt, unsafe, unwell or someone is being unkind, they tell a grown-up straight away.

Common mistakes: asking before trying, so help becomes a habit and the child never builds stamina; the opposite, sitting stuck and upset because asking feels babyish; vague asks such as I can't do it, which leave the helper guessing; and asking for the answer instead of a clue. Adults slip too, by jumping in with the answer the moment a child hesitates.

At home, when your child is stuck, ask what they have tried before you help, then give the smallest clue that gets them going. Praise the ask itself: good thinking to tell me what you tried. Say out loud when you are stuck and how you get help.

familyTip: Next time your child says "I can't do it", ask "What have you tried?" first. Then give one small clue, not the answer, and praise them for asking.

practice.prompt: Ella has tried {n} different ways to spell a word and is still stuck. What should she do now?
choices: ask a friend or a grown-up for a clue
practice.hint: She has already had a go. What is the next rung on the help ladder?
practice.explain: Ella has tried {n} ways, so now asking for a clue is the smart move.

practice.prompt: Before you ask for help with your work, what should you do first?
choices: have a go and try another way
practice.hint: Think of Pip and the word 'they'. What fixed it before anyone helped?
practice.explain: Have a go first. Often a new try or a clue on the wall gets you unstuck.

practice.prompt: Max is doing a {n}-piece jigsaw and is stuck. Which ask is clearest?
choices: I did the edges. Can you give me a clue for this corner?
practice.hint: A good ask says what you did and what you need.
practice.explain: Saying what you did on the {n}-piece jigsaw and asking for a clue tells the helper exactly how to help.

practice.prompt: Zara trips over and hurts her arm. What should she do?
choices: try to fix it herself first
practice.hint: Is this a stuck-on-work problem, or a hurt or unsafe problem?
practice.explain: When you are hurt, get a grown-up straight away. You do not need to try first.

pool.prompt: Is it OK to ask for help?
choices: Yes, after you have had a go
pool.hint: Do grown-ups ever ask for help? When is it smart?
pool.explain: Everyone gets stuck. Asking after you have had a go is what good learners do.

pool.prompt: Sam has been stuck on a sum for {n} minutes and feels cross. He has tried two ways. What now?
pool.hint: Look at the stuck meter in the lab. What happens if you sit stuck for a long time?
pool.explain: After {n} minutes and two tries, Sam should ask. Sitting stuck only makes him crosser.

pool.prompt: Why ask for a clue, not the answer?
choices: so you can finish it yourself and learn
so the helper does the work
pool.hint: Who does the learning if someone else gives the answer?
pool.explain: A clue lets you do the last bit yourself, so you learn it.

pool.prompt: Which of these needs a grown-up straight away?
choices: someone is being unkind to you
pool.hint: Hurt, unsafe or unkind problems are different from stuck-on-work problems.
pool.explain: If someone is unkind to you, tell a grown-up straight away. The others you can have a go at first.

pool.prompt: The teacher is busy reading with {n} children. You are stuck on a word but not hurt. What do you do?
choices: try the word wall or a friend, then ask when the teacher is free
pool.hint: You are not hurt, so it can wait a little. What can you try first?
pool.explain: The teacher is busy with {n} children, so try the wall or a friend, then ask at a good moment.

pool.prompt: What does a good ask say?
choices: what you are doing, what you tried and what you need
pool.hint: Remember the three lines in Pip's speech bubble.
pool.explain: A good ask says what you are doing, what you tried and what you need, so the helper knows how to help.

pool.prompt: Pip keeps trying the same way again and again. What should Pip do?
choices: try a different way, or ask
pool.hint: What happened to Pip's stuck meter when Pip did the same thing again?
pool.explain: Doing the same thing again does not help. Try a different way, and if that fails, ask.

pool.prompt: Leo asks for help before he even looks at the task. What might the helper say?
pool.hint: What did the teacher say when Pip jumped straight to the top of the ladder?
pool.explain: The helper asks what Leo has tried, so he has a go first.

visual.caption: Does it ask for a clue, or for the answer? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Which sound does it start with?
Can you show me the first step?
Is there a picture to help me?
Can you write it for me?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: help Pip climb the help ladder, build a clear ask, and sort problems into now or try first.
